clue.text: Who will volunteer in a big city matter?

definitions.note: The definition is put as a question rather than as a synonym: the answer is the word that answers it, the pronoun for no particular person.

parts.note: the clue's own single letter, taken exactly as it stands
NY is New York, the big city a setter reaches for when two letters are wanted
matter as opposed to spirit — the physical stuff a thing is made of

explanation.surface: A show of hands being called for over some piece of metropolitan business.
explanation.walkthrough: A call for a volunteer is answered by naming no one in particular, which is how a question can do a definition's job here.
explanation.definitionFit: 'Who will volunteer?' is answered by naming nobody in particular, and ANYBODY is exactly that pronoun — any person at all, chosen by none.

clue.text: Falls over climbing crag out of bounds

definitions.note: 'Falls' is plural and the answer is one place name, because the cataract itself is always spoken of in the plural.

indicators.note: Climbing goes upwards, and in a down entry that means these letters are read from the bottom of the answer towards the top.

parts.note: to do a thing over is to do it again, and that word is written upwards here

indicators.note: The bounds of a word are the letters at either end, and they are sent out, leaving only what sat between them.

parts.note: the pair left when the first and last letters of this word go

explanation.surface: A climber going over a cliff face somewhere off the permitted route.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Falls over' reads as one phrase about a tumble; the definition stops at the first word and 'over' is a piece of the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: Niagara is the great waterfall on the border between Canada and the United States, so 'Falls' defines it by the class of thing it is.

clue.text: Cash that folds inside turban knot essentially

indicators.note: Inside means already sitting within, so a run of consecutive letters is lying untouched in the words that follow.

parts.note: nine letters in a row, starting partway through the first word and running across two gaps

explanation.surface: Money folded away inside the knot of a turban.
explanation.walkthrough: A long hidden run is the easiest kind to walk past, because the eye reads 'turban knot' as one object and never spells it out letter by letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Banknotes are the paper half of money, the cash that literally folds into a wallet, as against the coins that do not.

clue.text: Commit seconds to advising Gen X?

indicators.note: A word's second is the letter standing in second place, and one is taken from each of the two words named after it.

parts.note: the letter standing second in each of these two words, in the order given
the X pencilled on a ballot paper is a choice cast, and the question mark flags that this is one use of the letter

explanation.surface: Someone spending their spare seconds handing out advice to Generation X.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Gen X' reads as one label for a generation and then splits in two, the Gen lending a letter and the X sending you off to a polling booth.
explanation.definitionFit: To devote time to a cause is to commit it there, and the two verbs take the same objects — commit an hour, devote an hour.

clue.text: In retrospect working both sides of casino is impossible

definitions.note: The definition is an adjective and the answer a spoken phrase: the setter swaps a word for the flat refusal that means the same.

indicators.note: Looking back over what has just been said, so in an across entry the letters are written out the other way, right to left.

parts.note: a machine that is working is on, and that little word is set down backwards

indicators.note: The sides of a word are its first and last letters, and both of them are wanted with nothing from the middle.

parts.note: the outer letters of the word are C and O, and calling for both of them — C and O — writes the joining word into the middle

explanation.surface: Someone who has been playing both ends of a casino thinking better of it afterwards.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Both sides' looks as though it can only ever hand over two letters, and the pair named as a pair carries an extra three between them.
explanation.definitionFit: NO CAN DO is the flat spoken refusal — it cannot be done — so the phrase stands in for 'impossible' as a whole idiom.

clue.text: Refined lead ore contains note — it's poisonous if ingested

definitions.note: The definition is a description, not a noun: the setter says what the thing does to you rather than naming the shrub it belongs to.

indicators.note: Refining ore breaks it down and casts it again, so the words beside it will not stay in the order they are printed.
What a thing contains sits within it, so the letter named next goes into the middle of the shuffled letters.

parts.note: anagram fodder, seven letters
n = note, the standard abbreviation, taken inside the shuffle

explanation.surface: A smelter turning out refined lead ore with something lethal mixed into it.
explanation.walkthrough: Lead is poisonous too, which is what holds the surface together and makes it easy to attach the definition to the metal instead of a plant.
explanation.definitionFit: Oleander is a common garden shrub whose every part is toxic to eat, so the clue defines it by its one notorious property.

clue.text: Record American left behind

parts.note: a = American, the standard abbreviation
l = left, as in stage directions or on a map
bum is the everyday British word for the backside, which is what a behind is

explanation.surface: An American who has been left behind somewhere.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole sentence reads as a note about somebody abandoned abroad, and its last word is the rude one — a setter's favourite, because 'behind' hides it so politely.
explanation.definitionFit: An album is a record in the sense of a released collection of songs, the disc a band puts out rather than a written account of events.

clue.text: Stays in ground instead

indicators.note: Grinding a thing reduces it to loose material, and letters ground down go back together in some new arrangement.

parts.note: anagram fodder, seven letters

explanation.surface: Staying on the ground as a substitute for whatever was planned.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stays' is the transitive verb here — to stay something is to hold it back — which is why a word about remaining can describe an act done to someone else.
explanation.definitionFit: To stay someone is to hold them where they are, the older transitive sense alive in 'a stay of execution', which is what DETAINS does.

clue.text: See 12 Across
This might help vehicle that's regularly going the wrong way

definitions.text: This might help vehicle that's regularly going the wrong way

indicators.note: Taken at regular intervals — the first, third and fifth letters of the word beside it, and none of the ones between.
The wrong way is the reverse of the right one, so in an across entry the pieces are written out from right to left.

parts.note: a van is one, and it arrives back to front
letters one, three and five of this word, the apostrophe ignored

explanation.surface: A driver who keeps taking wrong turnings and could do with some help.
explanation.walkthrough: Every word is working twice over: the sentence describes what the gadget is for while the same words hand over a vehicle and three letters to turn round.
explanation.definitionFit: A sat-nav is precisely the thing that helps a driver forever heading the wrong way, so the whole sentence reads straight as its description.

clue.text: Rather get away without minor inconvenience

indicators.note: Without is used in its old sense of outside — as in 'without the city walls' — so the piece before it wraps round the one before that.

parts.note: to flee is to get away, and the word opens up before its last letter
'rather cold' and 'a bit cold' say the same thing, so the phrase goes in whole

explanation.surface: Preferring to slip off rather than put up with a small annoyance.
explanation.walkthrough: The everyday 'without' meaning lacking is the trap: here the word is the archaic preposition for outside, and it carries the clue's only instruction.
explanation.definitionFit: A flea-bite itches for a moment and does no real harm, so the phrase stands for any inconvenience too small to be worth minding.

clue.text: Abroad with old newspaper — ambassador has issue 5

parts.note: somebody abroad is away
o = old, the standard abbreviation
the FT is the Financial Times, the pink-paper City daily and the crossword's stock newspaper
an ambassador is styled His or Her Excellency, shortened to HE on the envelope
the issue before a meeting is the question before it

explanation.surface: An envoy overseas with a back number of a newspaper, and a matter he wants raised.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is the bare number 5, which sends you to another clue for the meaning — a Guardian habit worth knowing, and easy to read as part of the sentence.
explanation.definitionFit: 5 across is the flat refusal that means it cannot be done, and this phrase says the same: a thing ruled out before anyone discusses it.

clue.text: Bob maybe in N. London borough

definitions.meaning: a bob is one particular cut, and 'maybe' flags it as an example of the wider thing rather than the thing itself
one of the local authorities at the top of London, out past Finchley and Hendon

explanation.surface: A man called Bob who lives somewhere in north London.
explanation.walkthrough: Barnet Fair is Cockney rhyming slang for hair, cut down to its first word the way rhyming slang always is, and the borough of that name is a real place.
explanation.definitionFit: In rhyming slang a barnet is a head of hair, and a bob is one style of it; Barnet is also a genuine borough of north London.

clue.text: Attendant doctor possessing perfect penmanship at the outset

indicators.note: What you possess you have about you, so the piece named first opens up and takes the next one into its middle.

parts.note: your hand is your handwriting — a fair hand, an illegible hand

indicators.note: At the outset means at the very start, so this piece goes to the front of the answer rather than where the clue names it.

parts.note: MD is the doctor's degree, and the two letters part company to make room
A1 means first-rate, and in a grid the 1 is written as the letter I

explanation.surface: A doctor who turns out to have beautiful handwriting.
explanation.walkthrough: Doctors' handwriting is the joke the surface runs on. 'At the outset' is not part of that description at all — it is the instruction sending the penmanship to the front.
explanation.definitionFit: A handmaid is a female personal servant, so 'Attendant' names her by the job itself: one who attends on somebody else.

clue.text: Unknown joining Disney to make music

indicators.note: Joining says the two pieces simply run together end to end, one written straight after the other.

parts.note: Disney's own first name, the man rather than the studio
algebra's unknown quantity is x, y or z, and only one of the three fits here

explanation.surface: A stranger teaming up with Disney to record something.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Unknown' is algebra's word rather than a mystery guest, and the two pieces arrive in the answer in the opposite order from the one the clue names them in.
explanation.definitionFit: A waltz is a piece in three-four time as well as the dance done to it, so 'music' names the tune rather than the steps.

clue.text: Crush West when revolutionary invades — being easily shocked

indicators.note: A revolution turns a thing full circle, so the name beside it is written out the other way round.
An invader forces a way in, so those letters end up inside the word already assembled rather than beside it.

parts.note: to squish a thing is to crush it, and this word splits after three letters
Mae West, the Hollywood star, lends her first name, and it turns round on the way in

explanation.surface: A revolutionary invading the West and crushing it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'West' is a person rather than a direction — Mae West, the 1930s film star — and the political surface is what keeps you reading it as territory.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone squeamish is turned queasy by blood or cruelty, so 'easily shocked' describes the same low threshold for anything unpleasant.

clue.text: Scandalmonger's best mate covers chest up

indicators.note: A cover goes over a thing and round it, so this word closes over the letters named after it.
In a down entry up means read from the bottom towards the top, so those letters run in the opposite direction.

parts.note: a mucker is British slang for a pal, and the word opens after three letters
an ark is a chest — the Ark of the Covenant was a box — and it is written upwards

explanation.surface: A gossip columnist's closest friend keeping his chest covered up.
explanation.walkthrough: Both halves of the surface change job at once: 'chest' is a box rather than a body part, and 'covers ... up' is two separate instructions with a word between them.
explanation.definitionFit: A muckraker digs up dirt about people and sells it, which is the trade a scandalmonger follows.

clue.text: Vegetating, comic Eric Morecambe is finally visiting Naxos on vacation

indicators.note: At the finish — the last letter of each word named before it, and nothing else from either.

parts.note: Eric Idle of Monty Python, one of two comic Erics the clue could mean

indicators.note: A visitor goes inside the house, so these letters sit within the piece named after them.
A place on vacation stands empty, so this word keeps only the letters at its two ends and loses everything between.

parts.note: the Greek island emptied out, keeping only the letter at each end
the last letter of each of these two words, in the order given

explanation.surface: Eric Morecambe holidaying on a Greek island and doing nothing much at all.
explanation.walkthrough: Two Erics collide: the surface hands you Morecambe, the great British comic of the seventies, while the wordplay wants Idle — and Morecambe keeps only his last letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Vegetating is doing nothing whatever, and idleness is the state of doing nothing, so the gerund and the noun name the same condition.

clue.text: Financial assistance from founders securing a little investment

definitions.note: The definition is a mass noun and the answer a plural: the help is counted as one lump of money rather than as the separate grants that make it up.

indicators.note: To secure a thing is to hold it fast, so the word beside it closes round the letter named next.

parts.note: a boat that founders subsides — goes down — and the word opens before its last two letters

indicators.note: A little of a word is not the whole of it — here only the letter it begins with.

parts.note: the opening letter of the word and no more of it

explanation.surface: Backers putting up a modest sum to keep something afloat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Founders' looks like the people who started the business and is really the verb — a ship that founders sinks — which is the whole difficulty in reading the first three words.
explanation.definitionFit: Subsidies are sums paid out to keep a service or an industry going, so 'financial assistance' is the category they belong to.

clue.text: Everyone can see this news about independent business run as symbol of Scotland

indicators.note: Round about — the letters named before it end up on either side of everything that follows.

parts.note: a film classified U is universal, passed for viewers of any age
n = new, and the plural asks for a second one, which is what leaves a gap between them
i = independent, as printed beside a candidate's name on a ballot
co = company, the abbreviation in half the firm names on a high street
r = run, the cricket scorer's abbreviation

explanation.surface: A story everyone can read about an independent firm and the way it is run.
explanation.walkthrough: Turning 'news' into two N's is the cheeky step: new is N, and the plural asks for more than one of them. The beast is Scotland's, chained on the royal arms.
explanation.definitionFit: The unicorn is Scotland's heraldic animal, facing England's lion on the royal arms, so the definition names it by what it stands for.

clue.text: Small PC close to price range

parts.note: s = small, as on the label in a shirt
a PC is a police constable, and a cop is the same officer in slang

indicators.note: The close of a word is its end, so only the final letter of the word named after it is taken.

parts.note: the last letter of the word

explanation.surface: A cheap little computer, priced to shift.
explanation.walkthrough: 'PC' reads as the machine on your desk and means the constable on the beat, and 'Small PC' looks like one description when it is two separate pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: The scope of a law or a job is how far it reaches, which is what a range is — the extent something covers.

clue.text: Compile 12 to make argument

indicators.note: The number sends you to 12 across, which supplies the word 'out', and letters that are out are no longer in the order they were given.

parts.note: anagram fodder, seven letters

explanation.surface: An instruction to put the answer at 12 together and start a row with it.
explanation.walkthrough: A cross-reference usually hands over letters; this one hands over the instruction instead, because the answer it points at is itself a word meaning out of order.
explanation.definitionFit: A polemic is a fierce written attack on a position, so 'argument' names it in the sense of a case pressed against something.

clue.text: See 27 Across
Particularly noxious six books on order

indicators.note: In an across entry a piece placed on another follows it, so the books come after the word for order rather than before it.

parts.note: six written in Roman numerals
a rule is an order handed down, and the two nouns swap freely
the New Testament, the crossword's usual books alongside the OT

explanation.surface: Half a dozen books waiting on an order at a shop.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Six books' reads as one quantity on an invoice, which is what keeps a Roman numeral and the Bible's second half from separating in your head.
explanation.definitionFit: A virulent disease or a virulent attack is poisonous in the extreme, so 'particularly noxious' catches both the sense and the force of the word.

clue.text: Two European articles below

parts.note: un is French for 'a', the first of the pair
der is German for 'the', the second of the pair

explanation.walkthrough: Continental languages keep a setter supplied with short words, and 'articles' is the signal to reach for a foreign 'a' or 'the' rather than an English one.
explanation.definitionFit: Under and below are everyday synonyms for a position lower than something else, and either word fits the same sentence unchanged.

clue.text: Uhura discovered characters bringing up the rear in red will die in difficulty

indicators.note: Taking the cover off a word leaves what was underneath, so the first and last letters go and the middle stays.
The character bringing up the rear is the one at the back, so it is the final letter of each word that is wanted.

parts.note: the Star Trek communications officer's name with the letter at each end taken off
the last letter of each of these three words, read in order

explanation.surface: The Star Trek crewmen in red shirts, the ones who never make it to the end of the episode.
explanation.walkthrough: Red shirts are the old Star Trek joke — the anonymous crewman beamed down in a red tunic is the one who dies — and Uhura wore red on the bridge herself.
explanation.definitionFit: A hurdle is a barrier to be got over, so it stands for any difficulty in the way — the figurative use of the racing obstacle.

clue.text: They're melting variety of cheeses with it

definitions.note: The definition is a statement about the answer rather than a synonym for it: the setter points at what these things are doing instead of naming them.

indicators.note: A variety is another form of the same thing, so the letters beside it come back arranged a different way.

parts.note: anagram fodder, seven letters
two more letters for the shuffle, lifted from the clue as they stand

explanation.surface: A cheeseboard left out too long, the whole selection going soft.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Variety of cheeses' is such a natural phrase that the instruction hides inside it, and 'with it' sounds like the rest of the same menu.
explanation.definitionFit: The polar ice sheets, the vast caps over Greenland and Antarctica, are the things famously melting, so the clue defines them by the news about them.

clue.text: Also manage to hold sign saying farewell

parts.note: also and too are the same word in different registers

indicators.note: To hold a thing is to keep it within you, so the word before opens up and takes the sign into its middle.

parts.note: to do is to manage — 'that will do' — and the word splits in two
Leo the lion is one of the twelve signs of the zodiac

explanation.surface: Someone managing to hold up a placard as well, on the way out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sign' has a dozen crossword meanings and the zodiac is the one setters reach for most, while 'to hold' carries the only instruction in the sentence.
explanation.definitionFit: Toodle-oo is a jaunty British goodbye, dated now but still heard, so the whole phrase stands in for a wave at the door.

clue.text: Originally, everyone sees knitting is my love language

indicators.note: The origin of a word is the letter it starts from, and the run of words after this one gives up one letter each.

parts.note: the opening letter of each of these five words in turn
love is nothing in tennis, and nothing is written as O

explanation.surface: Someone declaring that knitting is how they show affection.
explanation.walkthrough: Five initials in a row are hard to see when the words make a sentence that means something, and 'love language' is a modern phrase the surface leans on.
explanation.definitionFit: Eskimo names the language of the Arctic peoples — a term now usually avoided in favour of Inuit, but the one dictionaries still file the language under.

clue.text: Occasionally teenagers obsess and completely engage

indicators.note: Something done occasionally happens every so often rather than all the time — take every second letter and leave the rest behind.

parts.note: every second letter across both words, beginning with the second letter of the first

explanation.surface: Teenagers now and then getting fixated on something.
explanation.walkthrough: The two words have to be read as one continuous run, because the count carries straight over the space between them — which is what makes this kind of clue hard to spot.
explanation.definitionFit: To engross someone is to take up the whole of their attention, so 'completely engage' spells out the verb with its intensity included.

clue.text: Huge egg supplier in Germany — east of Berlin — I must get right involved

indicators.note: Said in Germany means said in German, so two of the words that follow are wanted in that language rather than in English.
Getting something involved brings it in among the rest, so the letter named lands inside the pieces already assembled.

parts.note: east as they say it in Berlin
r = right, the standard abbreviation
the German for 'I', which is what the clue's own pronoun turns into

explanation.surface: A German supplier of enormous eggs, somewhere east of Berlin.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In Germany' is doing translation work on two separate words a long way apart, and the dashes make the middle of the clue read as an aside about geography.
explanation.definitionFit: An ostrich lays the largest egg of any living bird, so 'Huge egg supplier' identifies it by the one thing it is famous for producing.
